source: Park, Leahey and Funk (2025 preprint of Nature reply) Robust evidence for declining disruptiveness
finding: Original authors rerun the Holst et al. critique on its own data and keep the finding: the decline in disruption stays large and significant. They say the zero-reference exclusion has no theory behind it.
numbers: Papers 1945-2010 N=22,456,096: beta -0.082 (p<0.001); patents 1980-2010 N=2,926,923: beta -0.155. SciSciNet has 2.76x (WoS) and 2.98x (PatentsView) as many zero-backward-citation works as the authors' data. CD=1 works: 4.3% WoS, 4.9% PatentsView, 23.1% SciSciNet. Variants (WoS decline in percentile points): CYG5 36, CD5^5 23, CD5^noK 16, binary Is-D5 about 7.5. Of 48 papers in both databases, 45 had references in WoS; references missing in WoS but present in SciSciNet 1.2%, the reverse 19.1%. Benchmarks: decline 15.53 points vs team-size shift 27.96.
limits: Authors' own side of the dispute (a party, not neutral). Holst et al. correctly found a plotting artefact in Extended Data Fig 1 (acknowledged). Variant names are CD5, CYG5, Is D5, CD5^noK, CD5^5, not DI5 or DI3%. Only first 100k characters read.
agent_relevance: Do not use any disruption variant as a label for rare high impact. The trend depends on data and zero-reference handling; the level of any single score is shaky.

source: Park, Leahey and Funk (2026) Reply to: Dataset artefacts can partially drive the measured decline in disruption, Nature 656:14-21
finding: Published reply exists (Nature, 2026, same day as the Holst et al. comment). Per INSEAD news, the team reran the critics' dataset, metric and model and says the decline remains.
numbers: No numbers read. Citation: Nature 656, pp14-21. Year taken from the INSEAD listing; sources differ slightly.
limits: Seen only in search results and an institutional listing; not opened. Closes 'reply not found' but not 'which variant is robust'.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: reply found. Both sides published; no neutral adjudication read.

source: Artiles et al. (2026) The Alien Space of Science: sampling coherent but cognitively unavailable research directions (NeurIPS 2026)
finding: Sampler picks combinations of idea atoms with high coherence and low availability to existing author communities. It gives far more distinct ideas than frontier LLM baselines at equal per-idea quality, and in an execution loop the LLM baselines collapse to one topic while the sampler does not.
numbers: Corpus 16,068 LLM papers. 300 ideas per method. Effective distinct ideas (Vendi): Alien 225.2; Claude independent 56.5; Claude batch-prompted 191.7 effective atoms vs Alien 198.0; near-duplicate share 81.7% (Claude batch) vs 51.3% (Alien). Human raters (10, 40 reviews): overall quality Alien 4.03 = Claude 4.03, Random 3.75, Gemini 3.68. Blind GPT-5.5 tournament, 50 ideas per method: Alien wins 55.6%, Gemini 54.4%, Claude 48.9%, Random 41.1%; after keeping the top half, Alien 72.2% vs Claude 27.8%. Autoresearch loop on 40 ideas (10 per method), 224 forced choices: mean rank percentile Alien 0.633, Claude 0.574, Gemini 0.495, Random 0.295. Interpretability-topic share: Claude 2/10 ideas to 8/10 reports; Alien 0/10 to 0/10. Judge-vs-expert agreement 68% (95% CI 54-80%) vs expert-expert 58% (50 raters, 10 report pairs). Predictive test on pre-2025 data: top <1% of candidates recovers 2025 combinations at 35.9x chance; with unavailability weighting, strictly novel combinations at 3.24x chance.
quote: directions that are coherent under the structure of existing knowledge, but that do not naturally arise from the conceptual trajectories of existing researchers
limits: Domain: LLM/ML papers only. LLM judge (GPT-5.5) in the loop. Only 10 ideas per method executed. Quality is rated, not citation or real-world impact. Needs a trained model over a literature corpus, not a pure prompt.
agent_relevance: Best new answer to gaps 1, 5 and 7: diversity must be built into the sampler, and homogenisation continues through execution (refinement pulls ideas to one attractor). Idea: sample explicit combinations with a 'who would already propose this' penalty.

source: Anchorless Diversification for Parallel LLM Ideation (2026)
finding: A planning call proposes 5 broad directions; the generation budget is split evenly across them. This raises diversity far more than prompting 'diverge', at 1.6x tokens for GPT-5.4. No reasoning-model-specific results.
numbers: Models GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro; 12 prompts (stories, alternative uses, slogans); 150 outputs per pool; 64,800 outputs total. Gain in mean pairwise distance vs independent neutral: 'diverge' alone 0.039 (GPT), 0.062 (Claude); stratified-diverge 0.172 (GPT) [0.162, 0.181], 0.253 (Claude), 0.134 (Gemini). Token ratio about 1.1 (diverge alone), 1.61 (stratified, GPT-5.4), 3.71 (peer2 multi-agent). Outputs needed to reach the neutral entropy target: stratified 7.4, diverge alone 17.9, neutral 72.6.
limits: Creative-writing and brainstorming tasks, not research ideas; quality by automatic proxies, no human or execution test; internal inconsistencies noted in the text (prompt counts, GPT peer2 vs strat figures). First 100k characters read.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partly closed: single-agent plan-then-split sampling gives about the diversity of multi-agent peer conditions at far fewer tokens. Tested at equal outputs, not fully equal tokens, and not with reasoning models.

source: Examining and addressing barriers to diversity in LLM-generated ideas (2026)
finding: Chain-of-thought plus personas raises the diversity of GPT-4o ideas to the level of, and by one metric above, a human sample. CoT reduces fixation in the LLM but not in humans.
numbers: GPT-4o; 10 fitness product ideas per participant; humans N=99 (Study 1) and 83 (Study 4). Full sample: human 28 categories / 197 combinations; LLM default 22 / 83; LLM+CoT 27 / 152; persona 27 / 193; persona+CoT 27 / 248 (about 26% above humans). Bootstrap (10 participants): persona+CoT 65.42 combinations vs humans 59.66, a much smaller margin. Fixation slope: default 1.013, CoT 1.363, ordinary personas 0.876. Between-participant spread: default 0.241, CoT 0.318, ordinary personas 0.635, entrepreneurs 0.429.
limits: One model (not a reasoning model), one domain, simulated participants, categories assigned by GPT-4o, one-sentence ideas. The 'beats humans' headline holds mainly on the full-sample metric.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 partly closed: sampled ordinary personas (not 'creative' ones) raised between-run spread most (0.635 vs 0.241). One model with sampled personas can mimic a group's spread of ideas; atypical combinations and value were not tested.

source: Li, Lin and Wu (2025) Can recombination displace dominant scientific ideas?
finding: In 41 million papers (1965-2024), atypical-combination papers (Uzzi measure) tend to have lower disruption. Atypicality marks extending established ideas into new topic areas; disruption marks replacing a dominant idea inside its own topic. The two measures capture different things.
numbers: 40,935,251 articles in the correlation analysis; negative correlation between atypicality and disruption; top-5% thresholds A > 22.9 and D > 0.04. Coefficients not extracted.
limits: Preprint; read intro, methods and figure captions only. Uses the disruption index, which is contested (d01). Frames K&V as the recombination side.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a large paper-data relative of K&V (wide combination is not the same as overturning a dominant idea). Not a replication of the patent topic result. Supports treating recombine and overturn as different operators.

source: Kaplan and Vakili replication search (this run)

numbers: No numbers. Related: Li, Lin and Wu 2025 (d06); Arts, Hou and Gomez 2021 NLP patent novelty (OpenAlex, 280 citations, not opened).
limits: Absence from a short search, not proof. A search summary called the sample nanotechnology patents (2,826), while earlier lines here say fullerene; check against the author PDF before quoting either.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open. Treat K&V as single-domain.

source: Si, Hashimoto and Yang (2025, ICLR 2026) The ideation-execution gap
finding: Re-seen in search: ICLR 2026 poster; same study as a21, b15, c05. No other-domain execution study with breakthrough-like impact appeared in the search results.
numbers: No new numbers (see a21: N=43 executors; AI ideas fell 1.05 novelty and 1.88 effectiveness points).
limits: Search snippet only this session; opened earlier in a21.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: still no non-NLP execution study measuring breakthrough-like impact.

finding: An automated executor runs LLM-generated ideas on two ML tasks, so outcomes are real training results, not ratings. Evolutionary search over ideas beats best-of-N, but RL on execution reward collapses idea diversity and raises the mean, not the maximum.
numbers: Tasks: nanoGPT speedrun (baseline val loss 3.255; 35.9 min to 3.28 loss) and GRPO on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B (baseline 48.0% on MATH). Execution rate over 90% for Claude-4.5 self-execution; same ideas run by GPT-5: 42-78%. 50 ideas per model: Sonnet 60.4% on GRPO; Opus loss 3.237. Evolutionary search: GRPO 69.4% at epoch 2 (human best 68.8%); nanoGPT loss 3.1407 and 19.7 min to 3.28 (human best 2.1 min). RL (Qwen3-30B-A3B): GRPO mean reward 0.253 to 0.343, nanoGPT 0.194 to 0.246; max reward flat; by epoch 68, 119 of 128 ideas were one of two patterns.
limits: Optimises effectiveness only, not novelty. ML-training domain, small scale, executor failures add noise. First 100k characters read.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 5, 7: first execution-grounded 2026 test with new models. Search with real feedback beats batch sampling; single-metric selection kills diversity, so keep tail candidates.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Serendipity by Design: cross-domain mappings and human and LLM creativity
finding: Forcing cross-domain mapping raises originality for humans but gives LLMs almost no average gain; for the strongest LLMs it helps only on the most distant pairs. Greater source distance predicts originality in both groups.
numbers: 140 human participants, 700 cross-domain and 700 user-need ideas; 7 LLMs (o3, Claude Sonnet 4, others); 1,002 raters, 2,800 ideas. Cross-domain effect b=0.36 (t=9.05); human-vs-LLM interaction b=0.48. o3 and Claude Sonnet 4 overall b=0.02 (p=.64); top 50% most distant pairs b=0.12 (p=.029); top 10% b=0.24 (p=.024). Distance beta: humans .10, LLMs .18. Originality vs feasibility r=-0.74; investment-worthiness tracks utility (r=.71) not originality (r=.23). Human-LLM pair-level originality r=0.44. LLMs used structural transfer more, humans surface transfer.
limits: One-shot, product design, lay raters, originality rated not realised value; LLM ideas were rated higher than human ones on originality, utility and investability.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 10 (partial): distance helps originality only when truly far, and feasibility drops as originality rises (r=-0.74). A far-seed operator should be gated on distance and followed by a feasibility check.

source: Zhang, Wang and Chen (2026) Scientific judgment drifts over time in AI ideation
finding: Experts rate the same idea differently over time. An ideation system aligned to first-wave ratings looked better until drift in human standards was removed; then the gain vanished. The idea generator pairs a conventional idea with a highly cited novel idea.
numbers: 63 researchers across 6 departments, 7,938 ratings, two waves; test-retest ICC 0.59-0.74 for overall quality on an identical control idea. Importance weights on originality, feasibility, clarity stayed stable.
limits: Quality ratings by researchers, not outcomes. No ablation of conventional-plus-novel seeding against all-novel or all-conventional seeding was read.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 not closed (no seed-mix ablation). Adds to K08: ratings are a noisy, drifting target, so fitting a selector to one snapshot overfits.

numbers: No numbers read (the PDF link returned 404 this session).

source: Idea Novelty Checker: literature-grounded novelty assessment of scientific ideas (2025)
finding: A pipeline of keyword plus snippet retrieval, embedding filter, then facet-based LLM re-rank judges novel or not novel with higher expert agreement than other agent novelty checkers. The facet-based re-rank is the part that matters.
numbers: 67 consensus-labelled ideas (39 novel, 28 not), 32 test. gpt-4o with 15 expert examples: accuracy 0.81, F1 0.79, kappa 0.59. AI Researcher (GPT-4o) 0.78 / kappa 0.52; AI Researcher (Claude-3.5) 0.56 / 0.19; AI Scientist 0.47 / 0.05. Ablation on known not-novel ideas (n=58): complete 89.66%; general RankGPT 13.79%; embedding only 10.34%; keyword only 5.17%. Expert agreement kappa 0.68.
limits: Tiny test set (32), same annotators wrote the examples, ideas from one generator (Scideator), only top 10 papers used. Text claims 13% higher agreement than AI Researcher, which the table (0.81 vs 0.78) does not clearly show.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 9 (partial): retrieval grounding plus a facet-aware re-rank is a workable prior-art filter. Plain embedding or keyword search almost never finds the prior art (10% and 5%).

source: Budgeted Subset Refinement for Execution-Aware LLM Research Ideation (2026)
finding: Abstract only. Raw generation and reranking alone gave zero research-strong non-duplicate ideas; refinement was needed. Diversity-aware subset refinement (MMR-k) gave the best yield, lowest duplicate rate and best cost per idea; random-k was a strong cheap baseline.
numbers: 10 random seeds, 10 ideation environments, blinded external-judge check on a balanced 72-item sample. Exact yields and costs not read.
limits: Abstract only. Proxy ratings under a fixed rubric; no execution outcomes (the paper says so); judge rankings among refined strategies disagree at item level.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 5: diversity-aware choice of which candidates get refinement tokens beats ranking alone, and random-k is a hard baseline.

source: IDEAgent: agentic quality-diversity search for research idea generation (2026, secondary summary)
finding: Per a secondary summary: a new idea competes only against its nearest neighbour in the active set; the loser goes to an archive, and rejected ideas go to a separate archive. This is a niche-based reserve.
limits: Blog summary of a paper not opened; details unverified.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a design pattern, not evidence that a reserve recovers tail wins.

finding: Per search summary: SciDER ranks ideas instead of scoring them because absolute LLM-judge scores are noisy and badly calibrated, and pins the best seed so re-ranking cannot displace it.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: weak support for ranking over scoring; no head-to-head against tournaments or Kelly-style scores found.

source: Search for tournament vs retrieval vs Kelly-style selector comparison (this run)
finding: No study compares pairwise tournaments, retrieval prior-art checks and past-vs-future novelty scores on the same LLM ideas against impact outcomes. Si et al. 2024 chose Swiss tournaments because pairwise ranking beat Likert scoring on a validation set (already a20, b14).
limits: Absence after several searches and fetches; either a real hole or not found.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open. Our own test would be the first comparison.
